name_b: Punctuation, newlines, and connectors that come right after a person's name (usually an author name or initial) in bylines, citations, and reference lists, marking where the name ends and the next element begins: commas, periods after initials, '.,', ' (' before a year, ' and', 'et al', semicolons, and line breaks before an affiliation or title. Activation is strongest after abbreviated initials in reference entries.

name_a: Hyphen/minus/dash characters and tokens naming them, usually as literal symbols in code strings, math, identifiers or separators (e.g. '-', "--", -*-, minus sign). The strongest hits are words for such punctuation ("hyphens", "hyphenated", "underscores"), with weaker hits on related naming conventions like snake_case and camelCase.
name_b: Subword suffix pieces completing technical names inside code, URLs, and config filenames, most strongly "-ci" in CI service names such as travis-ci and gitlab-ci, and weakly "ypi" in pypi. Isolated filler tokens in technical text activate only faintly.

name_a: The equals sign plus opening quote (=", =', =\") right after a "style" attribute in HTML/JS code, where inline CSS declarations are about to begin. Weaker on similar spots that open CSS values (.style, .css(', style.color = ").
name_b: CSS property names and their colons inside style declarations, especially inline HTML style="..." attributes (width, height, display, color, font-size, background-color, border, position). Values and units such as px get weaker activation, and the first property right after style=" activates most strongly. Similar styling or attribute keywords in other code (color, align, height) get weak activation.

name_a: Mainly the "al" in "et al." within academic author-year citations (strongest inside parenthetical references); weak activations on other predictable continuation tokens in structured/formatted text such as LaTeX backslashes, HTML table tags, section numbers in tables of contents, and abbreviation periods.
name_b: The "Answer" label (and its colon) placed after the lettered options of a multiple-choice question, right before the correct letter is given. It also fires more weakly on "Question" labels and on scattered tokens in synthetic, quiz-like or explanatory text.

name_a: Strongest on the hyphen or comma joining paired litigant role labels in legal case captions (e.g. 'Defendant-Appellant', 'Contemnor-Appellant', 'Defendant, Appellant'). It fires weakly on connective tokens in formulaic or boilerplate text, where the next word is highly predictable. Examples include the '?' line break after 'Still have questions', the 'weight' in 'weight loss', 'Do not' and 'Member, IEEE'.
name_b: Names of academic and research institutional units in author affiliations and bios, especially subunits like "Department of", "School of", "Laboratory", "Institute" or "Center" (including non-English forms), plus the field names and "University" that follow. Activation is highest on the unit word itself, such as "Department" or "School", and on the following "of", particularly in paper headers listing affiliations.

name_a: Prepositions and prepositional phrases that introduce a topic, meaning "concerning/with regard to" (e.g., "as to", "with respect to", "in regard to", "in relation to", "about", "regarding", "of"). The strongest activations fall on the topic-introducing word itself, especially "to" in "as to" and "respect"/"relation".
name_b: The definite article "the"/"The", mostly right after a verb or preposition (e.g. "of the", "in the", "request the") and often in formal, legal, academic or instructional prose. It also fires on sentence-initial "The" starting a new paragraph, such as "The following...". There are rare weak hits on non-article tokens.

name_a: Python traceback headers. Activation peaks on "back" in "Traceback", on the closing "):" of "(most recent call last):", and on the following indented "File" and its opening quote. Weak activation appears on other code/error contexts such as comment markers, imports and "Trace" in stack trace.
name_b: Words about creative authorship and composing, especially writing and composing music and songs (songwriter, composer, writing music, song-writing), plus related terms for writers, playwrights, designers, and creators. Activation is strongest for music and song writing.

name_a: Shell output redirection operators (>, >>, >&2) that send a command's output into a file or stream, usually right after an echo/cat string. Weaker hits are other output-directing constructs such as Python's print(..., file=), fputs(..., stdout), pipes, and file-creation commands like touch.
name_b: Shell I/O redirection syntax, chiefly the '>' operator (also '<', '>>', '&>', '2>&1') and redirect targets such as '/dev/null'. The strongest activations are on '>' or '>/' directly before /dev/null. Weaker activations fall on related command-line tokens like dd's if=/of=, file descriptor numbers, and output-file arguments.

name_a: Long runs of dot leaders (and similar filler like underscores or ellipses) that sit between an entry title and its page number, as in tables of contents or form fields. Activation is strongest on the first leader chunk after the title and drops on later chunks. Weaker activation appears on other separators between a label and its value, such as a <td> cell before a page number or a blank line after "Leave a Reply".
name_b: Dot leaders (runs of periods/ellipses, sometimes spaces or table cell tags) that fill the gap between an entry title and its page number in tables of contents, indexes and similar listings. Activation is strongest on the final dot tokens just before the page number.

name_a: The ".go" token appended to an identifier, firing hardest on Go source filenames (e.g. parser.go, app.go) and also on ".go" fragments inside URLs and domains (google, gov). Weaker activation on other file extensions like ".hs" and on stray dot or symbol tokens in code.
name_b: Tokens in formal document metadata and front-matter boilerplate, such as author bylines and affiliations, addresses, submission and acceptance dates, "Key words" and "Corresponding author" labels, DOIs and ID numbers, and case or bill numbers. Often the token is the line break that separates a header field from the following text, or the punctuation within these reference strings. A weaker, similar response appears for news datelines and name and score formatting.

name_a: Tokens inside institutional affiliation and address strings, typically from academic paper author headers. The strongest activations fall on the commas, connectors ("of", "and") and words like "University", "Department" and "Centre" that join nested units (lab, department, university, city). Weaker activation appears on similar organization-name text in prose.
name_b: Tokens that complete or continue the names of institutions and organizations, mostly research bodies, universities, academies, labs and government agencies (e.g. 'Academy of Sciences', 'CNRS', 'NASA', 'Fraunhofer Institute'). They typically appear in author affiliations, addresses and URLs. Activation is strongest on the later parts of these multi-token names and their acronyms.

name_a: Expository news-style prose. Activation peaks on the core clause of a sentence that introduces who did what, most often at the start of a new sentence or paragraph. Typical spans are the subject (a named person, organization or "The former couple"), the main verb, and the source-attribution phrasing that follows. Examples include "The attorney for … says in court papers", "According to a report produced by", "announced the split with" and "trimmed its … ownership in". Function words linking these elements (to, the, in, of, commas) are also marked, while scattered weak activations appear elsewhere.
name_b: No clear semantic theme; the feature fires on tokens that sit inside a fixed multi-token unit and are completed by what follows. These include subword pieces of identifiers, names and abbreviations (e.g. _FORCE in a constant name, the 'al' in 'Foal Eagle', '.g' in 'e.g.', 'sunshine' in a username). It also fires on whitespace indentation runs and on words in templated or spammy phrases.

name_a: The word "vein" and the related root "ven-" (venous, intravenous, venepuncture). Activation is strongest for anatomical blood vessels, especially "venous", and weaker for figurative uses like "in this vein" or "in your veins". It also fires weakly on other vascular and lymphatic terms (lymphatic, capillary, portal, phlebo-).
name_b: Middle-to-late terms of a descending sequence, mainly the low exponents (especially ^2, also ^3) and linear 'x' terms in polynomials written in decreasing-degree order, with strongest activation on the squared term. Weaker hits on other countdowns (5×4×3, 23…11, five/four/three) and indented rows of ASCII patterns that step down line by line.

name_a: Mostly weak, diffuse activation on technical and code text. It is strongest on CPU/assembly instruction mnemonics such as LD BC, ADD and NOP. Weaker activations hit command names, keywords and identifier fragments in code, shell commands and technical docs (e.g. rm, ssh, let, Dim, GET).
name_b: HTML form markup, strongest on the opening "<" of a new tag and on tag/attribute names like label, div and class="form-group"/"control-label" in nested form-group/label/input structures. Weaker, scattered activations fall on structural or transitional tokens in technical prose (colons before a breakdown, "for", "(", "from").

name_a: Mid-path segments inside highly predictable technical identifiers, chiefly ".bind" in Java/Spring package imports (org.springframework.web.bind.annotation, javax.xml.bind) and socket .bind calls. Also matches "/latest" in AWS documentation URLs, header names like <iomanip>, and acronym fragments (HTLV, AFJROTC). Weak activity on whitespace and newlines in templated bid listings and on ordinary function words.
name_b: Fires most strongly on the ".bind" segment of Java import paths (org.springframework.web.bind, javax.xml.bind) and on ".HttpServlet" in javax.servlet.http, i.e. a package segment within repeated import statements. Weaker activations occur on the optional-plural marker "(s" in form-style labels (Genre(s), Subject(s), Programme(s)) and on separators in repetitive boilerplate lists (semicolons in OEIS link lists, list dashes).

name_a: A diffuse, position-based feature with no single lexical trigger. It fires on tokens that sit just before, or inside, a specific identifying detail. Typical cases are separators and determiners leading into a name, institution, value or date: " -" before an author's affiliation or a location, "the" after "funded by", table <td> cells, "=" before a number, and year or date digits. It also fires on parts of proper names or codes.
name_b: A diffuse feature that fires on function words and punctuation at clause boundaries where a statement continues into a qualifying or elaborating segment. Typical triggers are prepositions (of, to, at, per), conditionals (if), an opening parenthesis, "e.g.," or a colon or newline. It shows up mostly in technical writing and code comments ("as per input convention", "Use actual weighting if known", "(e.g., ..."), but also on stray tokens in noisy or garbled text.

name_a: Tokens that end the fixed boilerplate or UI text of scraped web pages, such as "Jump to navigation, search", review/bid counts on freelance sites, "Need Help", "accept rate: %", "Google Scholar", timestamps, HAL IDs and ".com" in emails. They typically come right before a line break and the start of the page's actual content.
name_b: The word "reply"/"replies" (often split into subword pieces like "ply"/"plies") in web forum, blog, and mailing-list boilerplate UI text. Activation is strongest by far for "ply" in Blogger "noreply@blogger.com" email addresses, and weak for similar interface labels (improve this answer, edit, talk, CrossRef).

name_a: Tokens inside a repeated identifier that the model can predict by copying earlier context, most strongly the first subword pieces of custom package or namespace names in Java/C#/PHP import statements (e.g. com.<<.g>>em, se.<<.f>>idde, org.<<.d>>avidlin). Weaker activations fall on other repeated code identifiers, indentation, and recurring boilerplate or list patterns.
name_b: A separator plus the first fragment of an unusual or custom name that gets broken into pieces, such as a dot plus the opening letters of an uncommon Java package segment after "import com"/"org" (e.g. ".plan", ".y", ".m"), or a slash or dot plus the start of a URL path or domain. It also fires weakly on the backslash of \textsuperscript in affiliation lists.

name_a: Source attribution in news-style text: marks the cited person or organization behind a claim, firing most strongly on phrases like "according to [the police / the Ministry of Defence / a spokesman]" and "\", she said". It also activates more weakly on related cues such as agency and institution names (UN agency, ICE, National Ocean Service), job titles (secretary-general, spokesman), reporting verbs (say, said), and citation brackets or parentheses.
name_b: Spans of news-report prose, most strongly local incident and disaster reporting (accidents, fires, shootings, storm damage, attacks), where officials or investigators describe what happened and what was affected. Activation peaks on the narrative clause right after a paragraph break, such as "Investigators say the accident involved a truck and two cars". Elsewhere it gives weak, diffuse activation on ordinary factual reporting.

name_a: CSS and style-sheet code, chiefly property names (margin, padding, border, font-size, background, color) along with their colons, values and semicolons inside selector braces. The strongest activations are on layout and spacing properties like margin and border. It fires weakly on similar layout or formatting terms in prose and other code, such as size, margins, font and time listings.
name_b: Function words and punctuation that come right after a topic's subject or title is introduced, usually at the start of a definition or description ("X is a…", "X refers to…", "X has…", a comma or period closing the first descriptive clause). It fires on the verbs, relative pronouns, commas and periods that build an expository opening sentence about a named entity or term, often one just given as a heading.

name_a: Fires most strongly on the ".bind" segment of Java import paths (org.springframework.web.bind, javax.xml.bind) and on ".HttpServlet" in javax.servlet.http, i.e. a package segment within repeated import statements. Weaker activations occur on the optional-plural marker "(s" in form-style labels (Genre(s), Subject(s), Programme(s)) and on separators in repetitive boilerplate lists (semicolons in OEIS link lists, list dashes).
name_b: Mid-path segments inside highly predictable technical identifiers, chiefly ".bind" in Java/Spring package imports (org.springframework.web.bind.annotation, javax.xml.bind) and socket .bind calls. Also matches "/latest" in AWS documentation URLs, header names like <iomanip>, and acronym fragments (HTLV, AFJROTC). Weak activity on whitespace and newlines in templated bid listings and on ordinary function words.

name_a: Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.
name_b: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.

name_a: Separator tokens (spaces, newlines, double newlines, ">\n" in HTML tables, pipes, dashes) placed between items of a repetitive, predictable sequence, such as numbered pagination (1 2 3 4), number or year runs, alphabet indexes, figure labels, answer options, list entries, and table rows/cells. Activation is strongest deep inside long runs of structured, enumerated content.
name_b: Items in the middle of an enumerated or sequential list, typically after the first one or two. These are often successive numbers, letters, ordinals, months or coordinate components (y, z). Activation is strongest deep in predictable progressions like 1, 2, 3, 4 or A B C D…, and weaker for loose comma lists of related nouns such as countries, games or chemical classes.

name_a: Leading whitespace or indentation tokens at the start of a line, right after a newline, usually preceding indented content such as code lines, table-of-contents subsections (e.g. "2.1"), list items or continuation lines. Strongest for indented subsection entries in tables of contents and nested code. Occasionally fires on other line-initial markers (bullets, dashes, quotes) or trailing spaces before a newline.
name_b: The first token of a direct object or argument: a determiner, opening quote or parenthesis, or the first piece of a multi-token name or identifier. It typically follows a verb, preposition, or function call (e.g. print(lst, open TEST, into conf, the + noun). Activation is weak and diffuse, and is somewhat stronger for code identifiers and function arguments.

name_a: The word "cut" and its inflections (cuts, cutting, Cut) in any sense: literal slicing, reducing costs or amounts, phrasal verbs (cut off/down/back), idioms (cutting-edge, cut corners), and even as part of names or compounds.
name_b: The final digit of a year in a full date, typically a dateline or header at the top of a blog post, article or archive page (e.g. "Tuesday, May 8, 201[2]"). It fires most strongly when the date begins with a weekday name. There is weak activation on spaces after titles.

name_a: Separators between author names in academic author lists and citations. These are usually commas, but also semicolons, "and", "et" (as in "et al."), and punctuation fused with a closing bracket or period ("},", ".;", "),", ".,"). Activation is strongest for commas that follow an affiliation superscript in paper bylines.
name_b: Tokens within lists of person names, mostly author bylines of academic papers and citations. It fires on first names, initials, surname fragments and the separating commas or affiliation markers, and is strongest in the middle of long comma-separated author lists.

name_a: Highly predictable tokens inside fixed, boilerplate sequences, mostly in code: "ServletException" after "throws" in Java servlet methods, ".openapi" in package paths like com.intellij.openapi, and ".protocol" in location.protocol or web3j.protocol. It also fires on "eiusmod" in Lorem ipsum placeholder text. Activation is strongest where the token is nearly certain from context.
name_b: A single long whitespace token (a run of many spaces or tabs) used as padding or indentation. It shows up in code, tables, logs, ASCII art and garbled or noisy text, often right after a newline or a word and before more whitespace or content.

name_a: Sentence-ending punctuation (periods, often merged with paragraph breaks or closing parentheses) in formal academic, scientific, or legal expository prose, marking a boundary just before a new sentence or section. Discourse connectives that open the following sentence (e.g. "That is", "however", "but") and the first token after the break sometimes activate weakly.
name_b: Structural and formatting punctuation in document scaffolding. It fires most on periods in abbreviations and section numbers ("Fig.", "Jan.", "1. Introduction", "12.1.1") and on commas between citation numbers ("[7, 8]", "{1,2}"). It also fires on bullet-list leading spaces, section headers ("Abstract", "INTRODUCTION", "Index Terms"), superscript markup and boilerplate like "advertisement" or "navigation".

name_a: Strongest on the "(name" token, and to a lesser degree the following "=", in ORM column annotations in code (@Column(name=…), @JoinColumn(name =…)). Otherwise it gives only faint, diffuse activation. The most frequent weak cases are the indentation space before bullet (•) or numbered list items and line breaks inside lists. It also fires faintly on scattered words such as "Casinos" and "DirectX".
name_b: Street-level postal address components, mostly in academic affiliation or contact blocks. The strongest signal is on "PO Box"/"P.O. Box" and its number; street numbers, street-type words (Boulevard, place de, Drive, Bank) and nearby postcode digits, commas and hyphens also fire. Weak activations appear on fragments of place names and other non-address text.

name_a: Restrictive or exclusive focus words, mainly "only" (strongest when "Only" starts a sentence, e.g. "Only those" or "Only now"). They also fire on the determiner or quantifier that follows, such as "only the" or "only a few". Activation is weaker on related limiting or exceptive words like "except", "unless", "not until", "even" and "anything but".
name_b: A token that repeats one appearing just before it in a highly repetitive sequence (lists, loops, degenerate or glitchy text). It is strongest on placeholder, empty or negative values such as null, NaN, None, False, Empty, wrong and error.

name_a: Tokens that come right before a web address or file reference, mostly the URL prefix itself ("http", "://", "www", "<"), especially after phrases like "at", "see" or "online at" in license and contact boilerplate. It also fires weakly on punctuation or connectives that precede a new item.
name_b: Boundaries between clauses, sentences or code blocks: sentence-ending periods, closing brackets/semicolons, newlines and markdown fences, plus the first word or two of the next sentence or clause (The, This, If you, When you, For). Activation is highest where a statement or code block ends and a new one begins.

name_a: Subject-field words or word fragments, often abbreviated or split into subword tokens, within the names of academic journals, scientific societies, conferences and research departments in citations and affiliations (e.g. "Immun", "Micro", "Astr", "Endocrin"), especially the discipline term that follows "Journal of", "Frontiers in" or "and".
name_b: Separators and lead-ins inside lists of causes, conditions, diseases or factors. Fires on commas, 'and'/'or', 'such as', 'including', 'caused by' and 'signs of', and sometimes on the first word of the next item, at points where another item is about to follow. The lists are mostly medical, causal or diagnostic (e.g., 'caused by X, Y, or Z'; 'such as A, B and C').

name_a: Organization or institution names, often abbreviated, used as domain names in email addresses and URLs. The strongest cases are the part right after "@" in academic or research emails (kit, unipr, u-psud, tudelft, mit, inpe), with weaker activation on website domain parts and institution acronyms in credits.
name_b: Subword tokens that begin or form part of a multi-token word, where the next token completes it (e.g. "space" + "walk", "vapor" + "izers"). They often appear at the start of a sentence. The pattern is noisy: one case is a preposition leading into a hyphenated compound.

name_a: Function words, chiefly "of", directly following a plural noun and introducing its complement, as in "warranties of", "Schools of", "degrees of", "quantities of". Activation peaks on the license boilerplate "WARRANTIES OF" and the comment-prefix tokens on the next line. Other prepositions and connectives after nouns or verbs fire only weakly.
name_b: The word "indirect" in its various forms (indirect, indirectly, INDIRECT, or the "irect" piece of a split "Ind-irect"). It often appears in contrast with "direct" ("directly or indirectly", "direct and indirect"). There is also a weaker, constant activation on the backslash that opens a LaTeX command right after a display-math "\[" line break.

name_a: Long runs of whitespace (spaces or tabs) used as padding inside decorative comment boxes, ASCII banners, or tables, typically between border characters such as /* */, #, * or |. Activation is strongest for very long blank fills in comment-header borders. A few weak hits land on ordinary words or tags.
name_b: Diffuse, weak activation on words that start or carry a contrasting, concessive, or qualifying clause, i.e. a caveat or limitation on what came before. Typical carriers are "but", "even though", "although", "however" and "while". Hedges and negations also fire, such as "can be a challenge", "not going to", "possibly", "mainly" and "I would never say that". Peaks fall on the connective and the following few words, as in "but will not be", "but please keep in mind that" and "even though we remain".

name_a: The subword "toc" (or "oc" after T), strongest as the middle of "oxytocin" and in "toc" as a table-of-contents marker (e.g. {:toc}, toc = false, @[toc]); weaker for tocopherol, Tocqueville, Tocantins, and TOC.
name_b: Function words and predicate phrases directly following a named scientific entity (often a molecule, hormone, or chemical such as ATP, insulin, dopamine, or hydrogen) that describe its role or function, e.g. "is the key", "works as a regulatory molecule", "can be used as a", "responsible for", "played a role". Activation is weaker on scattered subword tokens inside technical names and acronyms.

name_a: The property or field name part of a setter method in code (the token(s) right after "set", e.g. setNeighbours, setId, setReduction), plus its parameter type and name. Weaker hits land on other method or field names and assignment parts of property setters.
name_b: Tokens that start the next item in a list of conditions or requirements, mostly in boilerplate legal, copyright, licensing and disclaimer text ("provided that X and that Y…"). The strongest activations fall on clause-linking words such as "that", "and", "and the" and commas, and on list bullets or dashes that begin a further stipulation.

name_a: Delimiter or boundary tokens that end a label or segment just before new content begins. The strongest are enumeration punctuation after list or option labels, such as the ")" in "(a)" or "(iii)" and the "." in "1." or "A.". Others are paragraph breaks after headings and spaces, slashes or braces that come right before a number or expression. Weaker activations fall on function words and adverb suffixes in garbled or spammy text.
name_b: Final class-name segments in Java import statements that name annotations (Spring, Lombok, JPA, Servlet, ButterKnife), especially Spring's ".Autowired", which fires strongly every time. Other annotation imports such as .Component, .Column and .AllArgsConstructor give weak activations. Non-import text produces only rare, faint hits.

name_a: The pronoun "it" after "modify" in the boilerplate free-software license phrase "you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms of..." (GNU GPL/LGPL, Perl license headers). Other weak activations are scattered, unrelated tokens.
name_b: The "/or" token in the phrase "redistribute it and/or modify it" from free-software license boilerplate (GPL/LGPL/Perl headers); other tokens fire only weakly.

name_a: Words naming behaviors, emotions, drives and physiological or psychological functions of organisms (feeding, eating, aggression, mood, motivation, fear, appetite, learning, memory, libido, responses), mostly in scientific or biomedical writing. The strongest hits are terms for behavioral and motivational processes. Weaker hits include cited author names in psychology and biology papers.
name_b: The second element of a hyphenated compound modifier (e.g., "-solving", "-energy", "-gas", "-quality"), i.e., the hyphen-prefixed token joining a word to the preceding word to form a compound adjective/noun modifier, usually before a head noun; weak scattered activations on other modifiers.

name_a: Whitespace/formatting tokens marking structural breaks between sections, mostly runs of multiple newlines (often with indentation or trailing punctuation) separating code blocks or paragraphs. Longer runs of blank lines, especially at the end of a document or before a new code or section header, activate most strongly. Odd or duplicated punctuation at boundaries (stray periods, quotes, commas) activates weakly.
name_b: Whitespace-only tokens, mostly runs of several newlines (often with indentation spaces or tabs), that form blank gaps between sections of code or documents. Activation grows with the length of the run, so long stretches of consecutive blank lines fire most strongly.

name_a: Speech and attribution markers in reported speech or news style: verbs of saying (said, added, reported, wrote, explained), the speaker or source named near a quote (he, she, Moscow, the report), and source nouns such as statement, release, interview, survey or papers. They mostly appear just after a quotation or claim, or in 'according to' constructions. The strongest activations are on 'said' and on source nouns like 'report', 'statement' and 'release'.
name_b: The preposition completing a source-attribution phrase, mainly "to" in "According to" and also "per" in "As per" or Dutch "volgens". It is strongest when "According to" opens a sentence and introduces a named source such as a person, organization or publication, and weaker after a lowercase mid-sentence "according".

name_a: Expository news-style prose. Activation peaks on the core clause of a sentence that introduces who did what, most often at the start of a new sentence or paragraph. Typical spans are the subject (a named person, organization or "The former couple"), the main verb, and the source-attribution phrasing that follows. Examples include "The attorney for … says in court papers", "According to a report produced by", "announced the split with" and "trimmed its … ownership in". Function words linking these elements (to, the, in, of, commas) are also marked, while scattered weak activations appear elsewhere.
name_b: The word "File" that opens a frame line in a Python traceback or stack trace (File "path", line N, in ...), usually right after "Traceback (most recent call last):" or a previous frame. Activation is strongest for later frames that follow code lines.

name_a: Timestamp and date fields in structured or machine output, firing most strongly on the size/date/time columns of Unix directory listings (ls -l), such as "40 Apr 20 13:03". It also responds to clock times (hh:mm:ss), the spaces between date parts and times, and year fragments like "200". Activations on ordinary prose are weak and scattered.
name_b: Whitespace or separator tokens (and the small number that follows) between fields in tabular, machine-generated text such as ls -l listings, process tables, DNS records, logs and version/download tables. It fires most strongly on the link-count number right after Unix permission strings (e.g. "drwxr-xr-x 2"). There is weak, scattered activation on other delimiters and punctuation.

name_a: The "#endif" preprocessor directive, strongest when it closes a header include guard at the very end of a C/C++ header file. Activation is weaker for mid-file #endif closing #ifdef/#else blocks and for template "endif" keywords in PHP or Django. Scattered weak hits on ordinary prose tokens are noise.
name_b: Function words (mostly prepositions like "by", "from", "with", "of", "according to", or verbs like "said"/"says") that come right before the mention of a person, group, or source. They fire where the text is about to name who said, did, made, or supplied something.

name_a: The word "Chicago" (including subword pieces like "icago"/"AGO") in any context: the city, institutions, teams, the musical, and especially the Chicago citation style. Weak activation on related items like "Bulls" or other city names.
name_b: Words naming an institution, organizational unit, program, service or facility (e.g. Extension, Institute, Department, Lab, Centre, office, programs, services), often the head noun or acronym tail of an organization's name, plus nearby text describing what the organization offers or does.

name_a: Location-related words, mainly "where" (and somewhere/anywhere/wherever), plus the clause that follows them, such as "where the physician holds their" or "Where are they". Activation is strongest on "Where" opening direct or indirect questions about a place ("Where can I", "where to go with"). It is weaker on locative relative clauses and on other wh-question phrases.
name_b: The " id" attribute name inside HTML opening tags (strongest right after "<div", especially for top-level container divs in body); weak sporadic activation on a few function words or bold markers in prose.

name_a: Separator tokens (colons, equals signs, opening quotes or braces, spaces) right after a property, parameter or field name and just before its value is written, especially color values in CSS, plotting and code (e.g. 'color:', "col = '", 'background-color: #'). It also fires more weakly on the space before a number in prose.
name_b: Language about self-perception, ego and status: people regarding themselves as superior, in charge or entitled, plus related notions of power, dominance, hierarchy, arrogance and ambition. The strongest cases are explicit attitude phrases such as "a superior attitude towards" and "see themselves as in charge." Weaker hits are scattered words about self-regard, confidence or how one thinks of oneself.

name_a: Mainly the bit-width number inside C/C++ fixed-size integer type names (the "32", "16", "8" in int32_t/uint32_t/uint16_t/uint8_t), plus other type-specifier tokens such as long, size, ull, int and float. Weaker activations land on the space after the dash before a username in Stack Exchange comment signatures ("– Name date").
name_b: Commas in postal addresses and institutional affiliations that come right after a city or locality name and come before the larger region (state, province, country) or the postal code.

name_a: Closing delimiters of code or template blocks, often merged with the newlines after them. The strongest case by far is PHP's closing tag "?>", especially when it ends a script. Weaker activations come from other closers such as Jinja/Django "%}", Handlebars "}}", code-fence backticks, triple quotes and XML declaration endings. There are scattered faint activations on ordinary prose words.
name_b: Opening delimiters that switch from literal text or markup into embedded code or expressions: PHP open tags (<?php) inside HTML, JSX braces ({) inside markup, and interpolation/placeholder markers in template strings (${, #{, {, {{, <%=, %, $). Strongest for <?php after HTML and JSX { inside elements.

name_a: Separators and items in enumerations of alternative values, chiefly "or", commas, "and", and slashes in phrases like "X or Y", "A, B, or C", or "either 1 or 8". It is strongest in chemical or math definitions that list allowed substituents or values, such as "represent hydrogen or methyl" or "K = ℂ or K = ℝ". It also fires weakly on the listed options themselves.
name_b: The "iggs" token completing the name "Higgs", firing most strongly in particle-physics contexts (Higgs boson, field, doublet, mass). It fires weakly for other "-iggs" surnames (Myers-Briggs, Griggs, Riggs), and there is faint, scattered noise on unrelated tokens.

name_a: The main verb or predicate, plus the words right after it, in titles, headings and questions, especially after "How to", "What is" or "Is it possible". It fires most strongly on action verbs that state the task or topic (filter, evaluate, replace, use, represent, administer).
name_b: Mostly fragments of biochemical signaling-molecule names, firing most strongly on "AMP" in cyclic AMP / cAMP, with weaker hits on related cyclic-nucleotide pathway terms. Related terms include GMP, c-di-GMP, phosphate, AMPK, PDE, adrenergic, second messenger, forskolin and theophylline. Weak, scattered activations also occur on lookalike acronyms (GMP certification, Accelerated Mobile Pages) and on paragraph breaks.

name_a: Double-newline paragraph-break tokens, typically with leading whitespace or punctuation fused in, that come right after a sentence or line ends and before a new paragraph, heading or code block. Activation is strongest when a space is fused before the break (" ⏎⏎") or the break falls after a math or code line.
name_b:
Sentence-final punctuation fused with newline(s) (e.g. ".

", "].

") marking the end of a paragraph, mostly in academic/scientific abstracts or papers, right before a new paragraph, section, or metadata begins.

name_a: Mostly titles or role labels that follow a person's name, particularly judicial designations such as the "J" in "Davis, J." and "Judge" in court citations, plus "Chair", "Editor" and "Secretary". Weaker hits fall on the last digit of years in dates and on list or structural punctuation.
name_b: Mostly the word "Judge" used as a title next to a person's name, especially in legal and court documents ("Signed by Judge X", "TANNENWALD, Judge:"). It also fires weakly on similar role labels attached to names, such as "Director", "J.", and "God", with occasional faint noise on unrelated tokens.

name_a: The final tab character in a run of leading indentation, i.e. the last whitespace token just before a line's content, mostly in code and structured data (JSON, XML/HTML, LaTeX, scripts). It fires most strongly on deeper or continuation indentation. A weaker version fires on single spaces or table cells ("<td") that come right before a new item or value.
name_b: Boundary tokens that close a self-contained block of boilerplate or header text, such as a license/copyright notice, file header comment, promo/signup blurb or disclaimer, just before new content begins. These are typically end punctuation fused with newlines ('.⏎⏎', ')⏎⏎', '⏎⏎') or comment-closing markers ('#⏎', '**⏎', "'''"). A few weaker hits fall on ordinary mid-sentence words.

name_a: Ordinal numbers within street addresses, especially the floor or street number such as "Fifth" or the suffixes "th", "nd", "rd" and "st" after a digit. Activation is far strongest on "Fifth" in the Free Software Foundation address ("51 Franklin Street, Fifth Floor"). Activations outside addresses are weak.
name_b: The subject of a reading-comprehension question, the word right after "What is/was" or "of". It is usually "the" or the noun it introduces, such as author, user, speaker, text or number, and is strongest for the person whose views are asked about ("the author's…", "the user's…").

name_a: Journalistic news-story prose, strongest on attribution and narrative-reporting phrases (e.g., ',” said X while attending…', 'he concluded, as reported by', 'shared:', 'Reportedly,') and clauses describing what a public figure did or is doing in celebrity, sports and news reports. Activation is weak and diffuse on other tokens.
name_b: A diffuse, weakly-firing feature with no single trigger token. It is strongest in biographical or news-style passages about a specific named person, often a celebrity, such as Bowie, Madonna ("Madge"), Kanye West or Obsidian. There it fires on the person's name, possessives, and pronouns or phrases referring to them and their circle ("his crew", "her father", "you"). Elsewhere it shows only scattered low activations on function words and punctuation.

name_a: Tokens that repeat or mirror an earlier token within a parallel, list-like or symmetric structure (e.g., the second item in a pair like "t1[1] == t2[1]", "eddie smith and joan smith", "opposite face", repeated values in parallel lines or code). The activation falls on the copied element that completes the parallel pattern.
name_b: Weak, diffuse activation on structural boundary tokens in formatted or code-like text: line breaks, closing brackets/braces followed by newlines, indentation whitespace, list numbering periods, table row tags, and the first token starting a new line, field, or list item. It marks the point where one structural unit ends and the next begins.

name_a: Words and word pieces expressing permanence, endlessness or long duration (eternal, enduring, perpetual, lasting, perennial, timeless, immortal, endless, infinite, lifelong). "Eternal" fires most strongly, and related mortality and age terms fire weakly.
name_b: Language describing transitions, contrasts or changes between two states, phases, categories or forms (e.g. "from liquid to plasma", "transition from first form to the second", "wet-to-dry", "chaotic or non-chaotic", "transformed into"), mostly in scientific or technical text. It fires most strongly on the connecting words (from, to, into, between, and/or, non-) and on the names of the contrasted states.

name_a: Whitespace, newlines, and structural delimiters (pipes, ampersands, backslashes, comment slashes, table cells) within spatially laid-out text such as ASCII diagrams, tables, LaTeX arrays/matrices, and figure labels. Activation is strongest on padding spaces and line breaks that align columns or box borders in multi-line 2D layouts.
name_b: Structural and formatting tokens inside tabular or grid-like layouts, such as cell separators (|, &, <td>), row starts after newlines, alignment whitespace runs, and dotted or dashed filler in markdown, HTML and LaTeX tables or matrices and ASCII-art blocks. Activation is strongest at the start of a new row or line within these structures.

name_a: Line breaks (and trailing markers like *, }, superscript-number syntax) right after the author-name list in academic paper headers, marking the transition to the affiliation block (Department, University, \textsuperscript{1}, "Affiliations:") or to the abstract. Weaker activations occur on similar header and metadata breaks.
name_b: Footnote and affiliation markers (superscript numbers, letters, asterisks, daggers, or LaTeX superscripts) that start a line after an author list in academic papers, introducing institutional affiliations or author notes. Weaker activation on similar note markers and on words like "Department" that begin an affiliation line.

name_a: A diffuse feature firing on mid-clause tokens (function words like 'and', 'of', 'to', 'him', verbs, and punctuation) where the sentence continues an action. It is strongest in classical Chinese biographical text and fires broadly on historical or biographical narrative about officials, emperors and generals, and on translated Chinese web-novel prose. It shows weak, scattered activation elsewhere, including scientific text, code and citations.
name_b: Tokens in East Asian (mainly Chinese) contexts: historical dynasties, figures, names, place names, romanized Chinese/Japanese words and their glosses, classical poetry and imagery, cultural items (food, calligraphy, gardens), and xianxia-style translated fiction. Peaks fall on Chinese historical and biographical descriptions and romanized names.

name_a: The noun right after a verb or modifier in short UI/share-button boilerplate and technical noun compounds, strongest on "article" in "Share article via email". It also fires weakly on "link" in "Copy link" and on compound heads like "security updates" and "module development".
name_b: The division slash (or decimal point / LaTeX \frac separator) inside a fractional number, especially in fractional exponents like ^(1/2), ^{1/4}, ** 0.5 for roots; weaker on plain fractions like 1/4 in lists.

name_a: Words for people or channels that covertly or confidentially supply information, such as sources, informants, contacts, tips/tip-offs, whistleblowers, undercover/double agents, and anonymous reports. Activation is strongest on "informant" and "tip-off".
name_b: The "www" subdomain token right after "http://" in URLs, firing most strongly in XML namespace URLs like xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" in SVG/HTML code. It fires more weakly on other URL hosts (googleapis, jquery's "code") and faintly on random tokens in code comments.

name_a: A diffuse, weak feature of scientific and technical expository prose (abstracts, papers, explanations in physics, materials science, biology, and math). It fires on scattered tokens within explanatory sentences: function words (the, of, that, is, with), clause-ending punctuation, and key technical nouns or phrases such as range, distance, phase transition and temperature dependence. It peaks on phrases describing physical quantities, conditions, or findings.
name_b: Language describing transitions, contrasts or changes between two states, phases, categories or forms (e.g. "from liquid to plasma", "transition from first form to the second", "wet-to-dry", "chaotic or non-chaotic", "transformed into"), mostly in scientific or technical text. It fires most strongly on the connecting words (from, to, into, between, and/or, non-) and on the names of the contrasted states.

name_a: Section/chapter numbering and identifier tokens in structured references: digits and separators in chapter/section numbers, LaTeX \label{sec:intro}/{s1} keys, figure filenames, DOIs, URL path IDs, and index codes. Peaks on the number or key that names a section or item (e.g. the "1" in \label{s1}).
name_b: Sentence boundaries inside memorized boilerplate legal and license text, peaking on the period and following space after "contributor license agreements" in the Apache license header (just before "See the NOTICE file"). Weaker activations appear at similar points in other stock phrases, such as the journal "page charges." disclaimer and other license wording.

name_a: Tokens containing the dollar sign "$" in any role: currency amounts, LaTeX math delimiters, shell prompts, and variable sigils in code (PHP, Perl, R, Rust macros, template ${...}). Activation runs highest for code and shell uses such as R's "\$" accessor, Perl comments, terminal prompts and PHP variables, and is weaker for plain currency and math.
name_b: A diffuse, mostly positional pattern rather than a semantic one. It fires on tokens sitting inside a fixed, highly predictable structure, where the next token is strongly constrained. These include separators inside phone numbers, the first halves of split compounds or set phrases ("game" before "pad", "in order" before "to", "w" in "w/w", "Program" before "Coordinator"), and double newlines after section titles or headings in technical and academic documents.

name_a: Words that open a hypothesis or setup statement, chiefly mathematical problem/proof language like "Suppose", "Let", "Consider", "Assume", usually at the start of a sentence before variable definitions (strongest for "Suppose"). Weak activations also appear on similar statement- or block-opening tokens such as code declarations (var, auto, public) and HTML <thead>.
name_b: Words that open a hypothesis or setup in mathematical/technical writing, chiefly "Let" (as in "Let X be…"), plus "Suppose", "Assume", "Consider", "If". They typically come at the start of a sentence or clause and introduce variables or premises. Activation is strongest for "let/suppose" right before a definition.

name_a: Fires on the subword "ember" (and close variants such as "umber", "ober", "amber", "bers", "bars") as a piece inside words or names, e.g. Ember, dismember, November/September, Pemberi, and surnames like Kemberly. It is strongest when "ember" sits mid-word in an unusual or foreign name.
name_b: Footnote and affiliation markers (superscript numbers, letters, asterisks, daggers, or LaTeX superscripts) that start a line after an author list in academic papers, introducing institutional affiliations or author notes. Weaker activation on similar note markers and on words like "Department" that begin an affiliation line.

name_a: Grammatical particles, case endings and inflectional suffixes in non-English text, especially Japanese particles (に, と), Korean postpositions (에, 로, 으로) and case or verb endings in agglutinative and inflected languages (Azerbaijani, Turkish, Russian, Latin). Activation is strongest on Japanese に and Korean 에.
name_b: The finite verb right after a sentence's subject, nearly always a form of "have" (has/have/had), mostly as a perfect-tense auxiliary ("has found", "have been") but also as possessive "has the right". Sometimes it is a form of "be" or a following "been". The strongest cases follow subjects like "I", "this study/research" or "the undersigned" in reporting or formal contexts.

name_a: A diffuse feature found in expository, advisory or policy-style prose about practices and processes, such as healthcare, management, public engagement and wellbeing. It fires on words that name means or approaches for achieving an outcome: nouns like methods, measures, steps, ways, tool, factors, involvement, engagement and communication, and action verbs like help, create, streamline, enhance, implementing and focusing. It also fires on nearby function words like "to", "in" and commas within those purpose and benefit statements. Activations are strongest on terms for participation and engagement and on tools.
name_b: A standalone space token that sits right before a number (a year, address number, ID, count, time, percentage, list index), usually following a comma, colon, dash, slash or the end of a name or title. It also fires on the leading space before bullet points or list items in metadata-like text such as citations, addresses, dates and listings.

name_a: The word "reasonable" and its variants ("reasonably", the "able" in "Reasonable"), most often in legal, contractual or policy phrases such as "reasonable doubt", "reasonable efforts/steps", "reasonable adjustments" and "reasonably believe". It fires weakly on related evaluative words like "fair" and "equal".
name_b: Weak, diffuse activation in tense or alarming narrative contexts, peaking on words describing fear, panic, worry or desperation (e.g. 'Panicking I began to try', 'heart dropped as she', 'feared', 'desperate') and on the reaction clauses around them. Elsewhere it fires faintly on function words, commas and verbs in emergencies, illness or death, urgent waiting or rushing.

name_a: Indentation whitespace at the start of the code line in a Python traceback, right after a 'File "...", line N, in func' header line (sometimes extending to the first keyword like raise/return or an '='). Weak activations on scattered punctuation and function words elsewhere.
name_b: Prepositional phrases and their referent objects after words like warranty, conflict of interest, liability, or correspondence. The feature fires on the relational preposition (regarding, as to, in relation to, concerning, about, for) and the following demonstrative and noun naming what the statement covers (this paper, these data, its licenses). It is strongest in boilerplate disclaimers and declarations.

name_a: Nouns that name a particular item or position within an ordered mathematical structure, chiefly "term" (also element, entry, series, numbers, side). It fires most strongly after ordinal or index phrases like "nth", "12th", "3rd" or "the 5th", as in "nth term of a sequence" or "5th entry in row 12". It also fires weakly on unrelated tokens in math or technical text.
name_b: Delimiter or lead-in tokens (colons, spaces, brackets, braces, "=", "of", "such as") right before an enumerated list or sequence begins, most often a sequence of numbers (series, arrays, number lists).

name_a: Final class-name segments in Java import statements that name annotations (Spring, Lombok, JPA, Servlet, ButterKnife), especially Spring's ".Autowired", which fires strongly every time. Other annotation imports such as .Component, .Column and .AllArgsConstructor give weak activations. Non-import text produces only rare, faint hits.
name_b: Induction/copying: fires on a word or subword that repeats one appearing earlier in the same text (names, acronyms, terms, numbers, code strings), usually at the start of the repeated phrase, where it can be predicted by copying the earlier occurrence.

name_a: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires mostly on unpredictable tokens in noisy or garbled text: OCR junk, mojibake, random alphanumeric codes and serial numbers, unit letters stuck to numbers, odd single characters or scripts, and gene or sequence strings. It also fires weakly on ordinary punctuation and line breaks in plain prose, which suggests it tracks high-surprise or out-of-distribution tokens rather than any one meaning.
name_b: Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.

name_a: Separator or connector tokens at the boundary between two parallel segments, marking where a second item, alias, gloss or field begins. Typical cases are opening parentheses before an explanation or alternate name, pipes, slashes, dashes, '#', ':', '; also' and 'or the'. Some hits also fall at the start of the next element in code, IDs, URLs or lists.
name_b: Words describing violent or physical events, motion, destruction and natural disasters: crashes, explosions, floods, plummeting, firing, attacks, collapse, ruins, projectiles. It is strongest on dramatic falling or impact sequences (e.g. a plane plummeting onto a house, crash landings). It also fires weakly on surrounding action verbs, connectives and some unrelated nouns.

name_a: Tokens naming the input or object that an operation is applied to, most often function parameters and argument variables in code (e.g. (array, (a, b, value, string, text, data, number). It also fires in prose for the thing being acted on or entered, such as "a given integer", "the amount in", "a set of", "enter a number", and "the substrate".
name_b: The word "gradient" in color/graphics contexts, firing most strongly on "-gradient" in CSS "linear-gradient(" and SVG gradient IDs. It fires weakly on other gradient mentions (SVG gradients, radial gradients) and barely on unrelated code tokens.

name_a: The tag name "body" inside an HTML closing tag (</body>), usually just before </html> at the end of a document. Other closing-tag names (main, div, container) fire weakly, and scattered unrelated tokens barely fire.
name_b: Tokens that close a structured block: HTML/XML closing-tag openers ", , ), the brace after LaTeX \end, final closing braces of code classes/functions, and "End"/#endregion. Also weakly fires on boundary text after a section ends (e.g., "Leave a Reply", list labels).

name_a: Variable symbols (mostly x, also y, n, X, etc.) in algebraic expressions, firing most strongly when the variable directly follows a numeric coefficient, as in the middle term of a polynomial (e.g. the x in "3x" within x² + 3x + 5). Occasionally fires on other math symbols after a coefficient or operator, such as sin, cos, ^ or exponents.
name_b: Numeric coefficients or constants in polynomial or algebraic expressions, mainly the third-position term after a plus or minus sign (e.g., the "6" in x³ − 4x² + 6x). It fires most strongly on the coefficient of the linear x term in cubic polynomials. Weaker activation appears on other numbers within sums or sequences.

name_a: Separators and markers that follow an author's name in a paper's author list, such as commas, "and", affiliation numbers, symbols like *, †, §, and the closing braces or $ of superscript markup. Activation is strongest on the comma or closing token right after the affiliation superscripts.
name_b: Words expressing decline or worsening of a condition or quality, peaking on the stem "deterior" (deteriorate, deteriorating, deterioration). Weaker activation on near-synonyms like degradation, degrade, decline, worsening, erode, disintegrate and detrimental.

name_a: The argument or subscript token right after a function or variable name in math and code notation, most often an opening bracket fused with a variable, as in f(x, a(n, R(t, x_i, row[i. It marks the start of a function's argument list or an index.
name_b: The opening argument or parameter token right after a function or operator name, typically a merged token like "(x", "(n", or "<T" that starts the argument list in math notation (f(x), a(n), P(S)) or code (function parameters, generic type parameters). Subscripts and indices right after a symbol also fire, more weakly.

name_a: Tokens in East Asian (mainly Chinese) contexts: historical dynasties, figures, names, place names, romanized Chinese/Japanese words and their glosses, classical poetry and imagery, cultural items (food, calligraphy, gardens), and xianxia-style translated fiction. Peaks fall on Chinese historical and biographical descriptions and romanized names.
name_b: A diffuse feature firing on mid-clause tokens (function words like 'and', 'of', 'to', 'him', verbs, and punctuation) where the sentence continues an action. It is strongest in classical Chinese biographical text and fires broadly on historical or biographical narrative about officials, emperors and generals, and on translated Chinese web-novel prose. It shows weak, scattered activation elsewhere, including scientific text, code and citations.

name_a: The "/wp" path segment (WordPress) in URLs and file paths, usually right after a domain or directory and before "-content", "-includes" or "-json". Weaker on standalone "wp"/"WP" tokens (e.g., "wpb-js-composer" CSS classes) and other URL path segments like "/media", "/node" and "/product".
name_b: Mostly function words and delimiters in the middle of a phrase or clause, such as articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, "to", "including/like/without", and colons or bullets in spec lists. Each typically sits just before the content word or value that completes the phrase (e.g. "even the [largest]", "forgets to [wear]", "Power Assist: [5 levels]"). The feature seems to mark connective tokens that anticipate a following complement rather than any specific meaning.
